Hook: In 1985 two economists, Rajnish Mehra and Edward Prescott, took the standard model of how assets are priced and fed it ninety years of American consumption. Then they asked what stocks should have paid over safe, short-term government bills. With patience and risk aversion in any range they thought sensible, the model's answer was at most 0.35 percent a year. The record, from 1889 to 1978, was 6.18 percent: stocks returned 6.98 percent a year after inflation, bills 0.80. The gap is a factor of about seventeen. They called it a puzzle, and forty years later it still has that name.

Why should anyone outside a trading floor care? Because the premium is the price of risk: what people demand for holding something that does badly in bad times. It sets the cost of capital, and so which factories, houses and ideas get built. It values pensions and insurance, and the long-run future in climate policy. And a model that cannot price it does not yet understand how people fear risk.

This part's question: what is a claim on the future worth, and how does that decide what gets built? How does a firm decide whether to build, and when to wait? What makes one asset pay more than another? And do prices track value, or run away from it?

One card before we start. This part is about how assets are priced and how the theories are tested. Its returns are history, and its trees and firms are models, not recommendations to buy or sell anything.
Economics, Built. Part twenty-three: capital and asset prices.

This part continues Act Five. You'll value a stream of dividends, and see how a firm decides how much to invest when building takes time and costs more in a hurry. You'll see why waiting can be worth more than building, and why, in a perfect market, how a firm is financed does not matter. You'll price a tree that bears fruit, and find that risk is priced by when it hurts. Then the puzzle, computed three ways, and three ways economists have tried to repair it. And whether prices move too much, bubbles in the laboratory, houses as assets, and the long-run return on everything.
Value: Chapter one. Present value and the Gordon formula.

Start with the arithmetic every asset price rests on. A dollar a year from now is worth one over one plus r today, where r is the rate at which you could grow a dollar instead. So an asset that pays dividends D one, D two, and so on, is worth the sum of their present values. That is the whole of the theory of value, if you know the dividends and the right rate. Both are the hard part. If dividends grow at a steady rate g, below r, the sum collapses to a famous formula: the first dividend over r minus g. John Burr Williams wrote down the idea in 1938; Myron Gordon made the formula a tool in the 1950s.

Take a share that will pay a dividend of 4 next year, growing 3 percent a year for ever. At a discount rate of seven percent it is worth four over four hundredths: 100. Raise the discount rate by a single point, to eight, and it is worth 80. One point on the rate, a fifth off the price. Long-lived assets, whose value lies mostly in the distant future, are extremely sensitive to the rate at which that future is discounted. That is why so much of what moves stock prices and house prices is not news about dividends or rents, but news about discount rates.

Here is the ratio in the record. Robert Shiller's data for the S and P composite index of American stocks, from 1871, the price divided by a year of dividends. In 1871 the market sold for about 17 times its dividends. On average, about 27. By 2012, about 42. Real dividends grew only about 1.3 percent a year. At the peak, in 2000, it touched 91. If the Gordon formula holds, a ratio that wanders this far means that either expected growth or the discount rate moved a lot. Chapter ten asks which.
Investment: Chapter two. Investment: the user cost and Tobin's q.

Now the firm, and what gets built. In 1963 Dale Jorgenson asked what it costs to use a machine for a year, even if you own it. The interest you could have earned on its price, plus the wear and tear, less any rise in what the machine will sell for; and the tax code changes all three. A firm should add capital until one more unit adds as much to output as it costs to use. On the Island, with interest at five percent and depreciation at eight, a unit of capital costs 0.13 a year. Lower the interest rate, or give the firm a tax break, and the user cost falls and the capital it wants rises. This is the channel through which interest rates move investment.

James Tobin gave the same idea a market price. Divide what the stock market says a firm is worth by what it would cost to rebuild its capital. Call that q. If q is above one, a new machine adds more to the firm's value than it costs, so build. Below one, do not. Firms do not jump straight to the capital they want, because building fast is expensive: installation, training, disruption. If those adjustment costs rise with the square of investment, the investment rate is q minus one over phi: proportional to how far q is above one. And Fumio Hayashi showed in 1982 that under constant returns, the q that matters for the next machine equals the average q that a stock market reveals.

Agora runs Hayashi's firm on the Island. Productivity rises by a fifth for good, which is the same, for the firm, as a fall in the user cost. The stock market sees it at once: q jumps to 1.48. The firm invests 12 percent of its capital in the first year, against the 8 percent that wears out. Capital climbs from 2.98 toward 3.91 over the next decades, and as it does, q falls back toward its steady value. Investment is a flow toward a target, and q is the market's measure of how far there is to go.
Option: Chapter three. The option to wait.

The user cost assumed a firm could sell a machine as easily as buy one. The textbook rule says build if the project is worth more than it costs. But most investment cannot be undone. A mine, a factory or a pipeline is sunk the day it is built. And most investment can be put off: next year you will know more about prices and demand. Building now kills the option to wait, and that option is worth something. Robert McDonald and Daniel Siegel priced it in 1986, and Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck made it a theory of investment.

Make it concrete. A project's value wanders up and down at random, with a given volatility. Building costs a fixed sum, once. The net present value rule says build as soon as the value passes the cost: the dashed line at one. The optimal rule is to wait until value exceeds cost by a margin that grows with uncertainty. With interest at four percent and a volatility of 10 percent a year, build at 1.42 times the cost. At twenty percent, at twice the cost. At forty, at 3.73 times. Waiting is not timidity. It is the price of an option that building would destroy.

This matters for business cycles. In 2009 Nicholas Bloom modelled firms with such options facing shocks to uncertainty itself. When uncertainty jumps, the threshold jumps with it, and firms pause hiring and investment all at once. As uncertainty fades, the projects that waited go ahead: a sharp drop and a rebound. So uncertainty about policy has a cost even before anything is decided. And investment in individual plants is lumpy, long waits and then bursts; whether that lumpiness survives in the aggregate is a question for Part fifty-two.
PlayIt: Chapter five. Play it: price a coconut tree.

Your turn. On the Island, next year will be good or bad, with equal chances. A coconut promised for next year, whatever happens, costs exactly one coconut today: the interest rate is zero. Now a tree. It will bear 20 coconuts if the year is good, and 0 if it is bad. On average, 10. How many coconuts would the Island pay for it today? A, six; B, eight; C, ten; or D, twelve. Pause, and choose.

Here is how the Island prices it. A coconut delivered in a good year, when everyone has plenty, is worth less to people today than one delivered in a bad year, when they are hungry: 0.8 against 1.2. These two numbers are the Island's stochastic discount factor. The safe coconut pays one in both years: half of 0.8 plus half of 1.2, exactly one. The tree pays twenty only in the good year, when coconuts are worth 0.8: half of sixteen, so 8. If you chose B, you were right. It is worth less than its average harvest of 10, because it pays when coconuts are least needed. A tree that paid twenty only in bad years would be worth 12, more than its average: that is insurance. So the tree returns 25 percent on average against the safe zero. That is a risk premium, and it comes from when the tree pays, not how much it varies.
Premia: Chapter seven. Risk premia and the consumption CAPM.

Now put a number on it. With power utility, marginal utility is consumption to the minus gamma, and for small changes the discount factor falls one for one with gamma times consumption growth. So the premium on any asset is approximately gamma, the coefficient of relative risk aversion, times the covariance of the asset's return with consumption growth. This is the consumption capital asset pricing model. Douglas Breeden derived it in 1979, and Lars Peter Hansen and Kenneth Singleton built the econometrics to test it.

Here is the formula on a century of American data, from Robert Shiller's series: real returns on the S and P composite and on one-year bonds, and real consumption per head. From 1889 to 1978, Mehra and Prescott's window, stocks returned 7.4 percent a year after inflation, bonds 1.7: a premium of 5.7 points. Consumption growth was smooth, a standard deviation of about 4 percent, and its correlation with stock returns about 0.57, so the covariance is tiny: 0.0046. The premium divided by the covariance gives the risk aversion the model needs: about 12, and over the longer span about 14. Most economists think a gamma between one and ten describes how people actually trade off risk. The stock market seems to ask for more, and Mehra and Prescott's calculation, next, shows the trouble runs deeper than one number.
Puzzle: Chapter eight. The equity premium puzzle, computed.

Mehra and Prescott did not just compute one number. They asked what the model could produce at all. Their economy's consumption grows 1.8 percent a year on average, up or down by 3.6 points, with a little persistence, matching the century's data. Agora solves it for every combination of patience below one and risk aversion up to ten, and plots each solution as a dot: the average safe rate it produces, and the premium. The record sits up here, a safe rate under one percent and a premium of 6.2. Among all the model's economies with a safe rate below four percent, the largest premium is 0.36 percent: their famous bound. To raise the premium, the model must raise risk aversion, and that sends the safe rate far off to the right.

In 1991 Lars Peter Hansen and Ravi Jagannathan found a sharper way to say it, with no model of consumption at all. Whatever the true discount factor is, its volatility relative to its mean must be at least the Sharpe ratio of any asset: its average excess return divided by the standard deviation of that return. For American stocks from 1889 to 2009, that ratio is 0.30. With power utility the discount factor's volatility is about gamma times the volatility of consumption growth, 3.6 percent. To clear the bar, gamma must be at least 8.2. Consumption is simply too smooth for anyone with ordinary risk aversion to demand six percent for holding stocks.

And raising risk aversion that far creates a second puzzle. With power utility, the safe rate is roughly impatience, plus gamma times expected growth, less a precautionary term. With gamma above eight and consumption growing two percent a year, the safe rate would be about 15 percent. In the record it was about 2. People that averse to risk are also unwilling to let their consumption grow, so they would want to borrow heavily against a richer future, and only a very high interest rate would stop them. Philippe Weil named this the risk-free rate puzzle in 1989. Power utility ties two things together, aversion to risk and willingness to substitute over time, that the data want apart.

That goes on the list of facts. Stocks have paid several points a year more than safe bills: six, in Mehra and Prescott's century, five and a half in Shiller's longer one. The standard theory can give a third of a point. Agora's column waits for the next chapter, which repairs the model three ways.
Repairs: Chapter nine. Three repairs: habits, long-run risk, disasters.

If the data are right, people must fear something the simple model leaves out. There are three leading answers. The first is habit. John Campbell and John Cochrane let people care about consumption above a habit level that follows their own past consumption. What matters is the surplus, the share of consumption above the habit, which wanders with luck: here a century of it, simulated with their calibration. When the surplus is thin, a small fall in consumption is felt as a disaster, and the price of risk soars: 0.51 at the average surplus, up to 1.14 after bad years. Stocks' Sharpe ratio of 0.3 fits comfortably inside. The premium then rises in recessions and falls in booms, which is also why, as chapter ten shows, returns are predictable over long horizons.

The second answer is long-run risk. Ravi Bansal and Amir Yaron let consumption growth carry a small component that is extremely persistent: a slow drift in the economy's growth rate. It is almost invisible in a few decades of data. With preferences, due to Larry Epstein and Stanley Zin, that separate aversion to risk from willingness to move consumption over time, people care intensely about news of the distant future. And stocks, claims on dividends far ahead, fall on exactly that news, so they must pay a premium. Its weakness is the mirror of its strength: the persistent component that drives everything is hard to find in the data.

The third answer is disaster. In 1988 Thomas Rietz suggested that stock investors are paid for the small chance of a catastrophe the century's American data happened not to contain. Robert Barro measured it in 2006 from the twentieth century's wars and depressions around the world: sixty disasters, about a 1.7 percent chance a year, with output per head falling on average by about twenty-nine percent. Agora gives the Island the same odds, with falls from fifteen to sixty-five percent. Without disasters, the premium stays near zero at any plausible risk aversion, in grey. With them, in red, it rises steeply. And the safe rate falls, because in a disaster a safe bond is what you want to hold. At a risk aversion of 3.5 the Island's premium is 5.1 percent with a safe rate of 2.3: both puzzles at once, with ordinary risk aversion. The price is a claim that cannot easily be tested: disasters are rare by definition.
Volatility: Chapter ten. Do prices move too much?

In 1981 Robert Shiller asked a simple question of the present-value formula. Here is the real price of American stocks since 1871. And here is what the market would have been worth if investors had known all the dividends that were actually going to be paid, discounted at a constant rate: the ex post rational price, P star. If the price is the best forecast of P star, it must vary less than P star, because a forecast cannot be more volatile than the thing forecast. It varies more: a standard deviation of 393 against 177. Prices swing far more than the dividends they promise can justify, unless the discount rate itself moves a great deal.

Where does the extra movement go? Into returns that can be forecast. Regress the next year's real return on today's dividend yield, dividends over price: almost nothing, an R squared of 0.03. Over the next five years, 0.15. Over ten, 0.24. When prices are high relative to dividends, returns over the following decade tend to be low. The windows overlap, so the long-horizon fits look better than their true precision, a trap that Part four would recognize. But John Campbell and Shiller showed the pattern is the same one as excess volatility: prices move because expected returns move, not because expected dividends do.

This is the efficient markets debate in one card. Paul Samuelson proved in 1965 that properly anticipated prices fluctuate randomly, and Eugene Fama organized the evidence that prices reflect what is known. Next year's return is indeed hard to forecast. But over a decade, prices that are high relative to dividends do predict low returns. Fama and Shiller, who disagreed about what that means, shared the Nobel prize in 2013 with Hansen. In Agora's reading, a premium that rises in bad times, like the habit model's, makes long-run returns forecastable without anyone leaving money on the table. The series' sister course, Quant, Built, takes up the evidence in depth.
Bubbles: Can a price stay above value even if everyone is rational? Split any price into the present value of its dividends, the fundamental, and whatever is left, a bubble. For people to hold the bubble, it must be expected to grow at the rate of interest, for ever. So it cannot exist on an asset with a last date, because at the last date it is worth nothing, and by backward induction worth nothing before. Nor can it grow faster than the economy for ever. Jean Tirole showed in 1985 that a rational bubble is possible only when the interest rate is below the growth rate: Part twenty-two's dynamically inefficient economy. Samuelson's money was exactly such a bubble: paper worth nothing in itself, held because the next generation will take it.

Bubbles appear even where everything is known. In 1988 Vernon Smith, Gerry Suchanek and Arlington Williams set up laboratory markets in an asset that paid a random dividend after each of fifteen periods, and nothing after. Its fundamental value falls in a straight line, and anyone can compute it: on the Island, the expected dividend is 24 cents, so the value starts at 3.60 dollars. In fourteen of their twenty-two markets, prices rose far above value and then crashed near the end. The Island's version needs only 7 traders of 12 who extrapolate the last price change: the price starts low, climbs past value, rides above it for half the session, and collapses as the end comes into view. Experience reduced bubbles in the laboratory, but did not end them.

Called it? In October 1929 Irving Fisher, then America's most famous economist, told an audience in New York that stock prices had reached what looked like a permanently high plateau. The market crashed within days. In Shiller's January figures the S and P composite was worth two-thirds less in 1932 than in 1929, three-fifths less after inflation, and it did not regain its 1929 real level until the 1950s. Wrong. Fisher's work on interest and money is still taught in Parts seven and twenty-eight. His forecast is taught here.
Housing: Chapter twelve. Housing as an asset.

A house is the largest asset most families own, and Jorgenson's user cost applies to it directly. Owning a home for a year costs the interest you could have earned on its price, the property tax, upkeep, and a premium for the risk of owning one large asset, less the rise in its price that you expect. James Poterba wrote it down in 1984. If owning and renting are both possible, they should cost about the same. So the ratio of price to rent is one over the user cost rate. It rises when interest rates fall, a Gordon formula for houses, or when people expect prices to keep rising: which is how expectations can feed a boom.

Here is the ratio for the United States: the national index of home prices divided by the consumer price index for rents, set to one in January 2000. Through the 1990s it barely moved. Then prices pulled away from rents, to a peak of 1.49 in 2006. They fell back to 0.94 by 2012. Since then the ratio has climbed again, to 1.36. Part of the 2000s boom was low interest rates, which the user cost says should raise the ratio. Part was expectations of further gains, which fed on themselves; and the bust that followed took banks with it, which Part thirty-three takes up.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: risk aversion, and investment's response to its cost.

Two dials. The first was opened in Part seven: relative risk aversion. Laboratory gambles over a few dollars give a fraction of one; consumption and labour supply about one; finance's estimates two to seven; survey gambles over lifetime income about four; the calibrations that fit asset prices, ten. This part adds three rows of its own. The Hansen-Jagannathan bound on Shiller's century needs at least eight. The consumption CAPM's premium over its covariance gives about twelve. And the Island with rare disasters fits the premium with three and a half. The status stays contested: the number you need depends on what you believe people fear.

The second dial is new: how much investment responds when the user cost of capital falls. Robert Chirinko, Steven Fazzari and Andrew Meyer used American firms in the 1980s, whose user costs differed, and found a small elasticity: about -0.25. Kevin Hassett and Glenn Hubbard's review in 2002 put the range of then-recent studies at minus a half to minus one. Eric Zwick and James Mahon studied bonus depreciation, temporary tax breaks for equipment, across a hundred and twenty thousand firms: eligible investment rose about ten percent in 2001 to 2004 and seventeen in 2008 to 2010, with small firms responding most, an elasticity of about -1.6. The status: contested. Whether a tax break or a rate cut builds factories depends on which of these is right, and on who is short of cash: the same lesson as Part twenty-two's households.
